Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.1

§1.1 What Is the Internet?

Nuts-and-bolts view, services view, RFCs, and protocol definitions

To understand the Internet, we examine it from two complementary perspectives: the nuts-and-bolts view (the physical hardware and software components) and the services view (the communication infrastructure enabling distributed applications).

🔩
1. Nuts-and-Bolts View

The Internet is an interconnected system of billions of computing devices called hosts or end systems. Hosts connect via a fabric of communication links (fiber, copper, radio, satellite) and packet switches (routers and link-layer switches).

🌐
2. Services View

The Internet is an infrastructure that provides services to distributed applications (Web, email, video streaming, games, social networks) through an Application Programming Interface (API) specifying how programs request data delivery from the network.

1.1.1 End Systems, Communication Links, and Packet Switches

  • End Systems (Hosts): Devices that sit at the network edge and run application programs. These include traditional PCs, workstations, and servers in data centers, as well as modern smartphones, tablets, TVs, gaming consoles, webcams, smart watches, and billions of Internet of Things (IoT) sensors. Hosts are divided into clients (e.g. mobile browsers) and servers (powerful machines in data centers).
  • Transmission Rate (Bandwidth): The speed at which a communication link pushes bits into the medium, measured in bits per second (bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps).
  • Packets: When an end system sends data, it breaks it into chunks and prefixes each chunk with header bytes. These formatted packages are called packets.
  • Packet Switches: Intermediate nodes that take an arriving packet on an incoming link and forward it onto an outgoing link. The two dominant types are:
    • Routers: Layer-3 switches typically used in the network core that read IP addresses to route packets between networks.
    • Link-Layer Switches: Layer-2 switches typically used in access networks that forward frames using MAC addresses.
  • Route / Path: The sequence of communication links and packet switches traversed by a packet from sender to receiver.
  • Internet Standards & RFCs: Internet standards are developed by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) and published as RFCs (Request for Comments). Examples include RFC 791 (IPv4), RFC 793 (TCP), and RFC 2616 (HTTP/1.1). Other standards bodies include the IEEE 802 committee (Ethernet, WiFi) and the W3C (Web standards).

1.1.2 What Is a Protocol?

📘 Definition: Network Protocol (Kurose & Ross §1.1.2)
A protocol defines the format and the order of messages exchanged between two or more communicating entities, as well as the actions taken on the transmission and/or receipt of a message or other event.

Every activity in the Internet is governed by protocols. For example, hardware protocols in network interface cards control bit transmission on copper or fiber; congestion control protocols in end systems regulate transmission rates; routing protocols in core switches construct forwarding tables.

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.2

§1.2 The Network Edge: Access Networks & Physical Media

DSL, Cable HFC, FTTH, Enterprise/Home networks, Wireless, and Transmission Media

The network edge consists of end systems that initiate and terminate data. An access network physically connects an end system to the first router (the edge router) on the path to any other end system.

1.2.1 Access Networks Comparison

Access Technology Physical Medium Architecture & Medium Type Typical Bandwidth Key Characteristics
DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) Telephone copper twisted pair Dedicated line to CO Up to 24–52 Mbps down, 3.5–16 Mbps up Uses FDM over copper: 0–4 kHz voice, 4–50 kHz upstream data, 50 kHz–1 MHz downstream data. Splitter separates voice/data at home; DSLAM multiplexes at Telco Central Office (CO). Speed independent of neighbors.
Cable Internet (HFC) Fiber to neighborhood + Coaxial to homes Shared broadcast medium Up to 1.2 Gbps down, 30–100 Mbps up (DOCSIS 3.1) Hybrid Fiber-Coaxial (HFC). Cable Modem Termination System (CMTS) at cable headend. Shared medium: multiple homes share the coaxial channel; heavy neighborhood downloads reduce available throughput.
FTTH (Fiber to the Home) Optical fiber Dedicated optical fiber 1 Gbps – 10 Gbps symmetric Two architectures: AON (Active Optical Network, switched Ethernet) and PON (Passive Optical Network). PON uses an Optical Line Terminator (OLT) at CO, passive unpowered optical splitters in the neighborhood, and an Optical Network Terminator (ONT) at each home.
Enterprise LAN (Ethernet & WiFi) Cat 5e/6 UTP copper + 2.4/5 GHz radio Star topology to Ethernet switch 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps wired; 100–1000 Mbps WiFi Hosts connect to an Ethernet switch via twisted pair. Wireless laptops and phones connect to an Access Point (AP) which wires into the enterprise switch.
Wide-Area Wireless (Cellular 4G/5G) Electromagnetic radio spectrum Cellular tower base stations 10–100 Mbps (4G LTE), 100 Mbps–1 Gbps (5G) Connects mobile devices within tens of kilometers to cellular base stations operated by telecommunication providers.
🎯 Exam Focus: Home Network Architecture
A typical home network connects multiple devices through a single integrated device (the "home router/combo box") that combines:
  1. An 802.11 Wireless Access Point (AP) for wireless phones and laptops.
  2. A 100 Mbps / 1 Gbps Ethernet Switch for wired devices (TVs, desktop PCs).
  3. A Network Router implementing IP forwarding and NAT (Network Address Translation) to share a single public IP.
  4. A Cable Modem or DSL Modem converting digital packets into analog signals on the access medium.

1.2.2 Physical Transmission Media

Bits travel across a physical medium as electromagnetic waves or optical pulses. Media are classified into two broad categories:

📡 Guided Media (Signals wave-guided in solid medium)
  • Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP): Two insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference. Cat 5e (100 Mbps / 1 Gbps up to 100m), Cat 6/6a (10 Gbps). Most prevalent in LANs.
  • Coaxial Cable: Concentric copper conductors separated by insulation. Offers higher data rates than twisted pair, used in cable TV networks and HFC broadband. Can function as a shared broadcast medium.
  • Fiber Optic Cable: Thin flexible strands of glass that conduct pulses of light (photons). Extremely high bandwidth (tens to hundreds of Gbps), low attenuation over tens of kilometers, and immune to electromagnetic interference. The backbone of core and transoceanic links.
📻 Unguided Media (Signals propagate freely through atmosphere/outer space)
  • Terrestrial Radio: Electromagnetic spectrum carrying signals via line-of-sight or reflection. Subject to path loss, multipath fading, and interference (WiFi 802.11, cellular 4G/5G, Bluetooth).
  • Satellite Radio: Relays signals between terrestrial ground stations:
    • Geostationary (GEO): Orbit at 36,000 km above equator. Stationary relative to Earth. Round-trip propagation delay is substantial (~280 ms one-way, ~560 ms round-trip).
    • Low Earth Orbit (LEO): Orbit at 500–1,500 km (e.g. Starlink). Much lower propagation delay (~10–30 ms) but constellations require hundreds of satellites because they move rapidly across the sky.

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.3

§1.3 The Network Core: Packet Switching & Circuit Switching

Store-and-forward, queuing delay, FDM vs TDM, and the hierarchical network of networks

The network core is the interconnected mesh of packet switches and communication links that transports data between end systems. There are two fundamental architectural paradigms for transporting data through a network of links and switches:

1.3.1 Packet Switching

End systems segment long messages into smaller chunks called packets of length L bits. Each packet is transmitted across a communication link of transmission rate R bits/second.

📘 Definition: Store-and-Forward Transmission
Most packet switches use store-and-forward transmission at link inputs. A switch must receive the entire packet (all L bits) before it can begin transmitting the first bit onto the outbound link.
🧮 Store-and-Forward Transmission Delay Equations
Transmitting 1 packet of L bits across a path of N identical links of rate R (separated by N - 1 routers, ignoring propagation/processing):
dend-to-end = N ⋅ LR
Transmitting P packets back-to-back across N links in a pipelined fashion:
dtotal = (N + P - 1) ⋅ LR

Queuing Delay and Packet Loss

Each packet switch has multiple links. For each link, the switch maintains an output buffer (also called an output queue). If a packet arrives when the outbound link is busy transmitting another packet, the newly arrived packet must wait in the output buffer (queuing delay). If the buffer memory becomes completely full, newly arriving packets have nowhere to be stored and are dropped (packet loss).

Forwarding vs Routing

  • Forwarding (Data Plane): The router's local hardware action of transferring a packet from an input link interface to the appropriate output link interface based on inspecting the packet's destination header and looking up the forwarding table. Occurs in nanoseconds.
  • Routing (Control Plane): The network-wide collaborative process that determines the end-to-end paths packets take from source to destination. Routers execute routing protocols (e.g. OSPF, BGP) to compute the values placed into forwarding tables. Occurs in seconds/minutes.

1.3.2 Circuit Switching: FDM vs TDM

In circuit-switched networks (e.g. traditional telephone networks), the resources needed along a path (buffers, link transmission rate) are reserved for the duration of the communication session. Dedicated transmission rate is guaranteed; no queuing delay occurs once connected.

  • Frequency-Division Multiplexing (FDM): The frequency spectrum of a link is divided among connections; each circuit receives a dedicated frequency band continuously.
  • Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM): Time is divided into recurring frames of fixed duration, each frame split into a fixed number of time slots. Each connection receives a dedicated time slot in each recurring frame.
🎯 Classic Exam Calculation: Packet Switching vs Circuit Switching Capacity
Suppose users share a 1 Mbps link, and each user generates 100 kbps when transmitting, but is active only 10% of the time (p = 0.10).
  • Circuit switching: Link capacity is partitioned into fixed 100 kbps slots:
    Max Users = 1000 kbps100 kbps = 10 users
    It can support at most 10 simultaneous users, even if all 10 are completely idle 90% of the time!
  • Packet switching: With 35 users, the probability that 11 or more users transmit simultaneously (causing queuing) is computed by the binomial distribution:
    P(X ≥ 11) = ∑k=1135 35k (0.10)k (0.90)35-k ≈ 0.0004  (0.04\%)
    Packet switching supports 3.5× more users with less than a 0.04% probability of experiencing any queuing delay!

1.3.3 A Network of Networks: The Internet ISP Hierarchy

End systems connect to access ISPs. How do access ISPs connect to one another? The global Internet is structured as a five-tier hierarchy:

  1. Access ISPs: Local and regional cable, DSL, or cellular companies connecting residential homes and enterprises.
  2. Regional ISPs: Intermediate networks connecting access ISPs to large backbone transit providers.
  3. Tier-1 ISPs: Global commercial transit backbones (e.g. AT&T, Lumen/Level 3, NTT, Verizon) that span continents with high-speed fiber trunks. Tier-1 ISPs connect directly to every other Tier-1 ISP without paying transit fees (peering).
  4. Points of Presence (PoPs): A group of routers in an ISP's network where customer ISPs can connect into the provider ISP.
  5. Multi-Homing: An ISP or enterprise connects to two or more provider ISPs to guarantee connectivity if one provider fails.
  6. Internet Exchange Points (IXPs): Third-party meeting points with high-speed switches where multiple ISPs peer directly with each other to exchange traffic free of transit charges.
  7. Content Provider Networks (e.g. Google, Akamai, Microsoft): Private networks that bypass the commercial public Internet by connecting their own private data centers directly to lower-tier ISPs via IXPs and peering.

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.4

§1.4 Delay, Loss, and Throughput in Packet Networks

The 4 components of nodal delay, the Caravan Analogy, queuing intensity, and bottleneck links

As a packet travels from source to destination across a network, it encounters four distinct delay components at every single node:

🧮 Total Nodal Delay Equation (§1.4.1)
dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop
  • Processing Delay (dproc): Time required by the router processor to examine the packet header, check for bit-level errors using checksums, and look up the forwarding table. Typically microseconds (μs).
  • Queuing Delay (dqueue): Time the packet waits in the output buffer queue before transmission begins. Depends on traffic intensity and preceding packets. Ranges from microseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Transmission Delay (dtrans = LR): Time required to push all L bits of the packet onto the physical link at transmission rate R bps. Depends strictly on packet size L and link rate R (independent of distance!).
  • Propagation Delay (dprop = ds): Time required for a single physical bit to propagate across the physical medium of distance d meters at propagation speed s (s ≈ 2 × 108 m/s in fiber/copper, 3 × 108 m/s in free space). Depends strictly on distance and physical speed of light (independent of packet size or link bandwidth!).
📏 Networking Units & Conversion Rules (Study Guide Page 20)
  • Data Size vs Rates: In networking, prefixes are powers of 10: 1 Kbps = 103 bps, 1 Mbps = 106 bps, 1 Gbps = 109 bps.
  • Bytes to Bits: Always multiply by 8! 1 Byte = 8 bits; 1 MB = 106 Bytes = 8 × 106 bits.
  • Time Units: 1 s = 1,000 ms = 1,000,000 μs; 1 ms = 10-3 s; 1 μs = 10-6 s.
  • Distance Units: Convert km to meters before dividing by s: d = 4,000 km = 4 × 106 m.
💡 The Tollbooth Caravan Analogy (Kurose & Ross §1.4.1 / Study Guide P4)
To intuitively differentiate transmission delay from propagation delay, consider a caravan of cars passing through highway tollbooths separated by a long highway:
  • Cars = Bits; Caravan = Packet; Tollbooth service rate = Link transmission rate (R); Highway = Link physical medium; Speed of car = Propagation speed (s).
Scenario 1 (Study Guide P4a): 8-car caravan, tollbooths 150 km apart. Each booth needs 15 s per car, cars travel at 100 km/h.
  • Time to push all 8 cars through first booth (dtrans): 8 × 15 s = 120 s = 2 minutes.
  • Time for the last car to travel 150 km at 100 km/h (dprop): 150 / 100 = 1.5 hours = 90 minutes.
  • Total time for entire caravan to line up before booth 2: 2 min + 90 min = 92 minutes.
Scenario 2 (Study Guide P4b - Superfast Cars): Cars travel at 1,000 km/h and a booth needs 1 minute per car.
  • First car leaves booth 1 at t = 1 minute. Travel time to booth 2 = 150 / 1000 h = 0.15 h = 9 minutes. First car arrives at booth 2 at t = 1 + 9 = 10 minutes.
  • Meanwhile, the 8th car leaves booth 1 at t = 8 × 1 = 8 minutes.
  • Does the first car reach booth 2 before the last car leaves booth 1? No! All 8 cars have cleared booth 1 at minute 8, well before the first car arrives at booth 2 at minute 10!

Queuing Delay and Traffic Intensity (L ⋅ aR)

Let a denote the average packet arrival rate (packets/second), L the packet length in bits, and R the transmission rate in bps. The dimensionless ratio:

Traffic Intensity = L ⋅ aR
  • If LaR ≈ 0: Packets arrive rarely; average queuing delay is practically zero.
  • As LaR → 1: Packets arrive in bursts faster than the link can drain them; queuing delay increases exponentially.
  • If LaR > 1: More bits arrive per second than the link can transmit. The queue grows without bound and packets are dropped (lost) when the router buffer overflows!

End-to-End Delay and traceroute

The program traceroute maps the route packets take between two Internet hosts:

  1. The source sends 3 UDP or ICMP probes with TTL = 1. The first router decrements TTL to 0, drops the packet, and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message (Type 11, Code 0) containing its IP address.
  2. The source records the round-trip time (RTT) for all 3 probes.
  3. The source increments TTL to 2, 3, 4, ... repeating the process until the destination host receives the probe and replies with ICMP Port Unreachable (Type 3, Code 3).
  4. Why can delay decrease between consecutive hops in traceroute? Internet routing is dynamic (probes take different paths), or intermediate routers deprioritize ICMP generation!

Throughput and Bottleneck Link

Throughput is the rate (in bits/sec) at which bits are delivered to the destination. For an end-to-end path with server link Rs and client link Rc:

Throughput = min(Rs, Rc)

The link on the end-to-end path that constrains the end-to-end throughput is called the bottleneck link. When N flows share a core link of capacity R:

Throughput = min(Rs, Rc, RN)

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.5

§1.5 Protocol Layers and Their Service Models

The 5-layer Internet stack, 7-layer OSI model, and packet encapsulation

Computer networks are exceedingly complex, comprising billions of diverse hosts, switches, copper/fiber/radio links, applications, and operating systems. To manage this complexity, network designers organize communication protocols into layers.

✈️ The Airline Travel Analogy (Kurose & Ross §1.5)
Consider taking an international commercial flight:
  1. Ticket purchase: Ticket counter / online booking.
  2. Baggage check: Checked baggage handlers.
  3. Boarding gate: Boarding pass scan & gate departure.
  4. Runway takeoff: Air traffic control runway clearance.
  5. Airplane routing: Aircraft en route to destination.
Each step performs an action and relies on the layer beneath it. If the airline upgrades its baggage barcode system, it does not require changing how air traffic control directs airplanes! Modularity allows updates without system-wide rewrites.

The 5-Layer Internet Protocol Stack

Layer Packet Name (PDU) Primary Function Example Protocols
5. Application Message Supports network applications; exchange of user messages between end systems HTTP, SMTP, IMAP, DNS, FTP, BitTorrent
4. Transport Segment Process-to-process data delivery, multiplexing/demultiplexing, reliability, flow/congestion control TCP, UDP
3. Network Datagram Routing datagrams from source host to destination host across network core IP (IPv4, IPv6), OSPF, BGP, ICMP
2. Link Frame Data transfer between neighboring network elements over a single communication link Ethernet (802.3), WiFi (802.11), PPP, DOCSIS
1. Physical Bits Modulates bits onto electromagnetic or optical transmission media 1000BASE-T, DSL, 802.11a/b/g/n/ac PHY
📘 The 7-Layer ISO OSI Reference Model vs 5-Layer Internet Stack
In the late 1970s, ISO proposed the 7-Layer Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model. It introduced two additional layers between Application and Transport:
  • Presentation Layer (Layer 6): Interprets the meaning of exchanged data (data compression, encryption, character conversion like ASCII/EBCDIC).
  • Session Layer (Layer 5): Delimiting and synchronization of data exchanges, checkpointing, and recovery.
Why does the Internet not have Presentation and Session layers? In the Internet architecture, these services are implemented directly inside the Application layer by application developers if needed (e.g. TLS encryption in HTTPS)!

Packet Encapsulation and Device Layering

As data moves down the protocol stack at the sending host, each layer adds its own protocol header (and sometimes a trailer) to the data received from the layer above:

Message M \xrightarrow{+ Ht} Segment (Ht + M) \xrightarrow{+ Hn} Datagram (Hn + Ht + M) \xrightarrow{+ Hl, Tl} Frame (Hl + Hn + Ht + M + Tl)

1. Application Layer (Message M)
The user application creates raw application data (e.g. an HTTP GET request message). PDU: Message.

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.6

§1.6 Networks Under Attack: Network Security Basics

Malware (viruses vs worms), Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS), packet sniffing, and IP spoofing

The original ARPANET was designed among a small community of trusted academic and military researchers. As a result, mutual trust was assumed and security was omitted from the core architecture. Today, malicious actors exploit this foundational openness:

1.6.1 Malware

  • Viruses: Malicious code that requires human user intervention to replicate and spread (e.g. opening an infected email attachment or executing a trojan program).
  • Worms: Self-replicating malware that spreads autonomously without any human action. A worm continuously scans the Internet for vulnerable hosts, injects itself into vulnerable processes over the network, and uses the newly infected hosts to scan and infect other hosts.
  • Spyware: Malware that secretly monitors user keystrokes, web browsing habits, and credentials, relaying them back to a collection server.
  • Botnets: A vast network of thousands or millions of compromised zombie hosts coordinated by a botmaster over IRC or P2P command-and-control (C&C) channels to launch coordinated attacks.

1.6.2 Denial-of-Service (DoS) and Distributed DoS (DDoS)

A DoS attack renders a network, host, or service unavailable to legitimate users. Kurose & Ross categorize DoS into three types:

  1. Vulnerability Attacks: Sending a few delicately crafted malformed packets to a vulnerable application or operating system, causing the host to crash or freeze (e.g. Ping of Death).
  2. Bandwidth Flooding: Flooding the victim's access link with an avalanche of bogus packets so that legitimate traffic cannot reach the server.
  3. Connection Flooding: Opening thousands of half-open or fully-open TCP connections (e.g. TCP SYN flood), exhausting the victim's OS connection buffers.

In a DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) attack, the attacker harnesses a global botnet to blast traffic simultaneously from thousands of disparate IP addresses, making source filtering nearly impossible.

1.6.3 Packet Sniffing & IP Spoofing

  • Packet Sniffing: A passive receiver placed on a shared broadcast medium (e.g. unencrypted WiFi, shared coaxial cable, hub Ethernet) puts its interface into promiscuous mode, recording a copy of every passing packet. Tools like Wireshark capture unencrypted passwords, credit card numbers, and emails. Defense: Strong end-to-end cryptography (TLS/SSL, SSH, IPsec).
  • IP Spoofing: Injecting a packet into the Internet with a false, forged source IP address. The receiver believes the packet originated from the spoofed trusted host. Defense: End-point authentication protocols (e.g. cryptographic nonces and digital signatures).

Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet • Section 1.7

§1.7 History of Computer Networking and the Internet

Milestones: Kleinrock's packet switching, ARPANET, TCP/IP Flag Day, Web explosion, and mobile cloud

The Internet evolved over more than six decades across five distinct developmental eras:

1. 1961–1972: Early Packet Switching & ARPANET

Leonard Kleinrock publishes the first paper on packet-switching queuing theory (1961). Paul Baran and Donald Davies independently conceptualize packet switching. First ARPANET node installed at UCLA (1969), connecting 4 universities via Interface Message Processors (IMPs). Ray Tomlinson writes first network email program (1972).

2. 1972–1980: Internetworking & TCP/IP

Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn release landmark paper (1974) outlining the TCP architecture for connecting disparate networks (DARPA Internetworking). Early network protocols (NCP) handled host communication.

3. 1980–1990: Proliferation & Flag Day

January 1, 1983 (Flag Day): ARPANET officially cuts over from NCP to the TCP/IP protocol suite. Mockapetris invents the Domain Name System (DNS) in 1983. Van Jacobson creates TCP congestion control algorithms (1988) following catastrophic Internet congestion collapses.

4. 1990s: The World Wide Web Explosion

Tim Berners-Lee invents HTTP, HTML, and URL at CERN (1989–1991). Marc Andreessen develops Mosaic (1993) and Netscape Navigator. NSFNET commercializes in 1995, transferring the backbone to commercial ISPs.

5. 2000s–Present: Mobile, Cloud & CDNs

Broadband residential access (DSL/Cable/FTTH), ubiquitous 4G/5G mobile connectivity, hyperscale cloud data centers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure), and Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) serving rich media to billions.

§1.8 Chapter 1 Summary & Exam Practice Problems (P1–P8)

Complete worked solutions to all 8 Midterm Study Guide Practice Problems plus Textbook Problems

Master these 8 practice problems from the official CPCS-371 Midterm Study Guide. Each question represents an exact exam pattern highlighted by the course instructors.

📝 Practice Problem P1: Networking Units Warm-Up
Study Guide P1

Problem: Convert the following quantities:

(a) Convert 3 MB to bits.
(b) Convert 2.5 Kbits to bytes.
(c) Convert 45 μs to ms.
(d) Convert 600 Kbps to Mbps.

(a) In networking, 1 MB = 106 bytes and 1 byte = 8 bits:
3 × 106 bytes × 8 = 24,000,000 bits  (24 Mbits)
(b) 2.5 Kbits = 2,500 bits. Divide by 8 to convert to bytes:
2,5008 = 312.5 bytes
(c) 1 ms = 1,000 μs:
451,000 = 0.045 ms
(d) 1 Mbps = 1,000 Kbps:
6001,000 = 0.6 Mbps
📝 Practice Problem P2: Transmission vs Propagation Delay
Study Guide P2

Problem: A 1,000-byte packet is sent over a 20 Mbps link that is 4,000 km long (s = 2 × 108 m/s).

(a) Compute the transmission delay and the propagation delay. Which one dominates?
(b) What is the propagation delay if the same link is only 400 m long? Which delay dominates now?

Part (a):
• Packet length in bits: L = 1,000 × 8 = 8,000 bits.
• Transmission delay:
dtrans = LR = 8,000 bits20 × 106 bps = 0.0004 s = 0.4 ms

• Propagation delay (d = 4,000 km = 4 × 106 m):
dprop = ds = 4 × 106 m2 × 108 m/s = 0.02 s = 20 ms

• Verdict: Propagation delay (20 ms) is 50 times larger than transmission delay (0.4 ms) and heavily dominates!
Part (b):
• For d = 400 m:
dprop = 400 m2 × 108 m/s = 2 × 10-6 s = 2 μs  (0.002 ms)

• Verdict: Transmission delay (0.4 ms = 400 μs) is now 200 times larger than propagation delay (2 μs) and heavily dominates! The two delays depend on completely different physical factors.
📝 Practice Problem P3: Store-and-Forward Pipelining
Study Guide P3

Problem: A host sends a 5,000-bit packet to a destination through one intermediate router. Both links have R = 1 Mbps. Ignore propagation, processing, and queuing delays.

(a) How long until the destination has the entire packet?
(b) The host sends three such packets back-to-back. When does the last packet arrive?

Part (a): Transmission time per link:
LR = 5,000 bits106 bps = 0.005 s = 5 ms
Because the router must store the entire packet before forwarding:
dtotal = 2 × LR = 2 × 5 ms = 10 ms
Part (b): Pipelined transmission of P = 3 packets over N = 2 links:
• Time t = 0 to 5 ms: Host sends Packet 1 to router.
• Time t = 5 to 10 ms: Router forwards Packet 1 to destination; Host sends Packet 2 to router.
• Time t = 10 to 15 ms: Router forwards Packet 2 to destination; Host sends Packet 3 to router.
• Time t = 15 to 20 ms: Router forwards Packet 3 to destination.
dtotal = (N + P - 1) ⋅ LR = (2 + 3 - 1) × 5 ms = 4 × 5 ms = 20 ms
📝 Practice Problem P4: Tollbooth Caravan Analogy
Study Guide P4

Problem: An 8-car caravan travels between tollbooths 150 km apart. Each booth needs 15 s per car, and cars travel at 100 km/h.

(a) How long after the caravan starts at the first booth is it lined up before the second booth?
(b) Now cars travel at 1,000 km/h and a booth needs 1 min per car. Does the first car reach the second booth before the last car has left the first booth?

Part (a):
• Transmission time for all 8 cars through first booth: 8 × 15 s = 120 s = 2 minutes.
• Propagation time for the last car on the highway: 150 km100 km/h = 1.5 hours = 90 minutes.
• Total time until caravan lines up at booth 2: 2 min + 90 min = 92 minutes.
Part (b):
• The first car is serviced at booth 1 in 1 minute, departing at t = 1 min.
• Travel time for the first car: 150 km1,000 km/h = 0.15 hours = 9 minutes.
• The first car arrives at the second booth at t = 1 + 9 = 10 minutes.
• Meanwhile, the 8th (last) car leaves booth 1 at t = 8 × 1 min = 8 minutes.
• Answer: No! All 8 cars have departed booth 1 by minute 8, which is 2 minutes before the first car reaches booth 2 at minute 10!
📝 Practice Problem P5: Traffic Intensity and Queuing Loss
Study Guide P5

Problem: Packets of 500 bytes arrive at an average rate of 300 packets/sec at a router output link of 1 Mbps.

(a) Compute the traffic intensity and describe what happens to the queue.
(b) What is the highest average arrival rate that keeps the traffic intensity at 0.5?

Part (a):
• Packet length in bits: L = 500 × 8 = 4,000 bits.
• Traffic intensity:
I = L ⋅ aR = 4,000 bits × 300 packets/s106 bps = 1,200,0001,000,000 = 1.2

• Verdict: Because I = 1.2 > 1, more data arrives than the link can service. The queue buffer will fill up, queuing delay becomes unbounded, and newly arriving packets are dropped (packet loss).
Part (b): To achieve I = 0.5:
a = 0.5 ⋅ RL = 0.5 × 106 bps4,000 bits = 125 packets/second
📝 Practice Problem P6: Path Throughput and Bottleneck Link
Study Guide P6

Problem: A server sends data to a client over a server link Rs = 3 Mbps and a client link Rc = 8 Mbps.

(a) What is the end-to-end throughput, and which link is the bottleneck?
(b) The server link is upgraded to 12 Mbps. What is the new throughput and the new bottleneck?

Part (a):
Throughput = min(Rs, Rc) = min(3, 8) = 3 Mbps
The server link (Rs) is the bottleneck link.
Part (b):
New Throughput = min(12, 8) = 8 Mbps
The client link (Rc) is now the new bottleneck link.
📝 Practice Problem P7: Circuit Switching (TDM vs FDM)
Study Guide P7

Problem: All links have a rate of 2.048 Mbps and use TDM with 32 slots. Setting up an end-to-end circuit takes 250 ms.

(a) How long does it take to send a 480,000-bit file over one circuit?
(b) If the links used FDM with 32 frequency bands instead, at what rate would each call transmit?

Part (a):
• Transmission rate per dedicated circuit:
Rcircuit = 2.048 Mbps32 = 2,048 kbps32 = 64 kbps = 64,000 bps

• Transmission time for the 480,000-bit file:
dtrans = 480,000 bits64,000 bps = 7.5 seconds

• Total elapsed time including circuit set-up delay (250 ms = 0.25 s):
dtotal = 0.25 s + 7.5 s = 7.75 seconds
Part (b): With FDM with 32 bands, each call transmits at 2.048 Mbps32 = 64 kbps. The difference is that in FDM, the 64 kbps bandwidth is available continuously, whereas in TDM it transmits in periodic time slots.
📝 Practice Problem P8: Protocol Layering & Security Threats
Study Guide P8

Problem:

(a) Which layers are implemented in an end system host, in a router, and in a link-layer switch?
(b) Give the official name of the packet (PDU) at the Transport, Network, and Link layers.
(c) Explain the difference between a virus and a worm, and explain why broadcast media are vulnerable to packet sniffing.

Part (a):
• Host: Implements all 5 layers (Physical, Link, Network, Transport, Application).
• Core Router: Implements layers 1–3 (Physical, Link, Network).
• Link-Layer Switch: Implements layers 1–2 (Physical, Link).
Part (b):
• Transport layer: Segment.
• Network layer: Datagram.
• Link layer: Frame.
Part (c):
• Virus vs Worm: A computer virus requires human intervention (such as downloading and running an infected attachment or program) to replicate and execute. A worm is self-replicating and autonomously spreads across the network without user intervention.
• Packet Sniffing Vulnerability: On a shared broadcast medium (such as wireless radio or shared coaxial cable), physical signals reach all interfaces in range. An adapter set to promiscuous mode can intercept, copy, and log all passing frames, capturing unencrypted data.
📝 Textbook Problem: Bandwidth-Delay Product & Reception Time
Kurose & Ross P8

Problem: Suppose two hosts, A and B, are separated by 20,000 kilometers and connected by a direct link of rate R = 2 Mbps. Propagation speed is s = 2.5 × 108 m/s.

(a) Calculate the bandwidth-delay product, R ⋅ dprop.
(b) Consider sending a file of 800,000 bits from A to B. How long until the first bit arrives at B? When is the file completely received?

Step 1: Distance d = 20,000 km = 2 × 107 m.
dprop = ds = 2 × 107 m2.5 × 108 m/s = 0.08 s = 80 ms
Step 2: Bandwidth-Delay Product:
BDP = R × dprop = (2 × 106 bps) × 0.08 s = 160,000 bits
Physical significance: The link "pipe" can hold up to 160,000 bits in transit simultaneously!
Step 3: The first bit arrives at B after exactly dprop = 80 ms.
Step 4: Transmission delay:
dtrans = LR = 800,000 bits2 × 106 bps = 0.4 s = 400 ms
Step 5: Total reception time until the last bit is received:
dtotal = dtrans + dprop = 400 ms + 80 ms = 480 ms  (0.48 s)

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.1

§2.1 Principles of Network Applications

Application architectures, communicating processes, sockets, and transport requirements

At the core of network application development is writing programs that run on different end systems and communicate with each other over the network. Crucially, application software runs strictly on end systems; you do not write software that executes inside network-core packet switches or routers.

2.1.1 Application Architectures: Client-Server vs P2P

Dimension Client-Server Paradigm Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture
Server Characteristics Always-on host with a fixed, well-known IP address. Scalability requires massive data centers. No dedicated central server. Arbitrary pairs of connected end systems communicate directly.
Client / Peer Role Clients do not communicate directly with each other; they only contact the server. Peers are both consumers and suppliers of service. A peer is a client when downloading, and a server when uploading.
Scalability Server bandwidth bottleneck as clients grow; high infrastructure cost. Self-Scalability: Each new peer brings new upload capacity as well as new service demand.
Host Connectivity Server has fixed IP, 24/7 uptime; clients have dynamic IPs and intermittent connectivity. Peers are intermittently connected and change IP addresses dynamically (high churn).

2.1.2 Processes Communicating Across the Network

In operating systems terminology, an executing program is a process. When two processes communicate across different hosts, they do so by exchanging messages through a software interface called a socket.

🚪 The Socket Interface (The Door Analogy)
A socket is the software interface between an application-layer process and the underlying transport-layer protocol stack.
  • A process is analogous to a house, and its socket is analogous to its front door. When a process wants to send a message to another process, it pushes the message out its door into the network.
  • Control boundary: The application developer controls everything on the application-layer side of the socket (message format, timing, application logic). The developer has very little control over the transport-layer side, limited only to: (1) choosing TCP or UDP, and (2) setting a few transport parameters such as buffer sizes and maximum segment sizes.

Addressing Communicating Processes

To deliver a message to a specific process running on a remote host, the sending host requires two pieces of addressing information:

  1. IP Address (32-bit in IPv4): Identifies the specific destination host across the global Internet.
  2. Port Number (16-bit integer, 0–65535): Identifies the specific receiving process / socket on that destination host. Why is the IP address alone not enough? Because a single host runs dozens of network processes simultaneously (web server, email server, SSH daemon, browser)!

2.1.3 What Does an Application-Layer Protocol Define?

An application-layer protocol defines how application processes running on different end systems pass messages to each other:

  1. Types of messages exchanged: (e.g. request messages and response messages).
  2. Syntax of message fields: How fields are delineated and formatted (e.g. ASCII strings terminated by CRLF).
  3. Semantics of the fields: The meaning of the information contained in the fields.
  4. Rules: Determining when and how a process sends messages and responds to messages.

Protocols defined in RFCs (such as HTTP, SMTP, DNS) are open protocols that guarantee interoperability between different software vendors. In contrast, proprietary protocols (like Skype or Zoom) use closed formats.

2.1.4 Transport Service Needs of Network Applications

Different applications have vastly different transport requirements along three dimensions:

  • Data Loss: Some applications (file transfer, Web, email, banking) require 100% reliable data transfer (zero loss tolerated). Multimedia applications (conversational audio/video, live streaming) are loss-tolerant (a dropped packet produces only minor visual or audio glitch).
  • Throughput: Bandwidth-sensitive applications (video streaming, VoIP) require a minimum guaranteed throughput to be effective. Elastic applications (email, file download, Web browsing) can utilize whatever throughput is available without failing.
  • Timing / Delay: Interactive real-time applications (Internet telephony, video conferencing, multiplayer games) require low latency (tens to hundreds of milliseconds) to feel conversational. Delay is non-critical for elastic file transfers.
🎯 Transport Service Requirements Table (Kurose & Ross Table 2.1 / Study Guide P10)
Application Data Loss? Throughput Guarantee? Time Sensitive? Typical Transport Protocol
File Transfer / Download No loss tolerated Elastic No TCP
Web Browsing No loss tolerated Elastic No (few seconds) TCP
E-Mail No loss tolerated Elastic No TCP
Internet Telephony (VoIP) Loss-tolerant Audio: 64–128 kbps Yes: 10's–150 ms UDP or TCP
Interactive Real-Time Games Loss-tolerant Few kbps–100 kbps Yes: 10's–100 ms UDP or TCP

2.1.5 TCP vs UDP Services and What TLS Adds

  • TCP Service Model: Connection-oriented (3-way handshake), 100% reliable in-order byte stream, flow control (prevents sender overflowing receiver buffer), and congestion control (throttles sender when network core is congested). Does NOT provide: timing guarantees, delay guarantees, or throughput minimums.
  • UDP Service Model: Connectionless (no handshake), lightweight, unreliable best-effort data delivery. No flow control, no congestion control. Allows applications to pump bits as fast as desired.
  • Securing TCP with TLS (Transport Layer Security): Neither TCP nor UDP provides any encryption; cleartext passwords sent over standard TCP are vulnerable to packet sniffing. TLS/SSL is implemented at the Application layer (using TCP underneath) to provide end-to-end encryption, message integrity, and endpoint authentication.

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.2

§2.2 The Web and HTTP

HTTP message formats, persistent connections, cookies, web caching, and HTTP/2 & 3

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the Web's application-layer protocol (RFC 1945 for HTTP/1.0, RFC 2616 for HTTP/1.1, RFC 7540 for HTTP/2, RFC 9114 for HTTP/3). A Web page consists of objects (base HTML file, JPEG images, CSS stylesheets, JavaScript files) addressable by a Uniform Resource Locator (URL):

\underbrace{http://www.someschool.edu}Host name  /  \underbrace{someDepartment/home.index}Path name
📘 HTTP is a Stateless Protocol
An HTTP server maintains no state about past client requests. If a client requests the same object twice in a few seconds, the server resends the entire object from scratch without remembering the previous request.

2.2.2 Non-Persistent vs Persistent HTTP Connections

  • Non-Persistent Connections (HTTP/1.0 default): Each TCP connection is closed immediately after the server sends the requested object. Fetching a page with 1 base HTML file and 10 JPEG images requires 11 separate TCP connections!
    Response Time per Object = 2 × RTT + dtrans
    (1 RTT for TCP 3-way handshake + 1 RTT for HTTP GET request and first bytes of response).
  • Persistent Connections (HTTP/1.1 default): The server leaves the TCP connection open after sending a response. Subsequent requests and responses between the same client and server can be sent over the same ongoing TCP connection.
    • Persistent with Pipelining: The client sends requests as soon as it parses referenced objects, back-to-back without waiting for prior responses. All referenced objects can be retrieved in roughly 1 RTT total!
Figure 2.1 — Timeline of TCP 3-Way Handshake followed by HTTP/1.1 persistent request/response exchanges (§2.2.2).

2.2.3 HTTP Message Formats (Command-Line Dissection)

HTTP messages are human-readable ASCII text strings. There are two types: request and response.

🎯 High-Yield Exam Dissection: HTTP Request Message Format
GET /cpcs371/notes/ch2.html HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: www.example.edu\r\n
Connection: keep-alive\r\n
Keep-Alive: timeout=5, max=100\r\n
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)\r\n
Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,ar;q=0.8\r\n
\r\n
  • Request Line (Line 1): Has three fields:
    1. Method: GET (requests an object). Other methods: POST (uploads user form data in the entity body), HEAD (requests identical headers without the body, used for debugging), PUT (uploads an object to the specified path), DELETE (removes an object).
    2. URL Path: /cpcs371/notes/ch2.html (path on server disk).
    3. HTTP Version: HTTP/1.1.
  • Host: www.example.edu: Mandatory in HTTP/1.1! Required for Web proxy caches and virtual hosting, where multiple domain names share the same physical server and public IP address.
  • Connection: keep-alive: Informs the server that the client wants a persistent connection. (Set to close if non-persistent).
  • Keep-Alive: timeout=5, max=100: The server should close the idle connection after 5 seconds of inactivity, and service at most 100 requests over this single connection.
  • User-Agent:: Identifies client browser and OS (used for server content negotiation).
  • Empty Line (\r\n): Marks the end of the header section.
🎯 High-Yield Exam Dissection: HTTP Response Message Format
HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Date: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 07:31:00 GMT\r\n
Server: Apache/2.4.52 (Ubuntu)\r\n
Last-Modified: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT\r\n
Content-Length: 6821\r\n
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8\r\n
\r\n
<html><head>...</html> (Entity Body)
  • Status Line: Protocol version (HTTP/1.1), 3-digit status code (200), and phrase (OK).
  • Common HTTP Status Codes:
    • 200 OK: Request succeeded and requested object is in entity body.
    • 301 Moved Permanently: Requested object relocated; new URL specified in Location: header.
    • 304 Not Modified: Conditional GET response; cached copy is up to date, entity body is empty!
    • 400 Bad Request: Generic error code; server could not understand request.
    • 404 Not Found: The requested document does not exist on this server.
    • 505 HTTP Version Not Supported: Server cannot speak the requested HTTP protocol version.
  • Date:: Time the server created and transmitted this response (NOT when file was last edited).
  • Last-Modified:: Timestamp when the object was created or last modified on server disk. Critical for caching!
  • Content-Length:: Size of entity body in bytes (tells persistent connections where object ends).
  • Content-Type:: MIME type of payload (e.g. text/html, image/jpeg).

2.2.4 User-Server Interaction: Cookies

Because HTTP is stateless, websites use cookies to track user state (shopping carts, user identity, recommendations). The cookie technology has four components:

  1. A cookie header line in the HTTP response message: Set-Cookie: 167845.
  2. A cookie header line in subsequent HTTP request messages: Cookie: 167845.
  3. A cookie file stored on the user's host and managed by the browser.
  4. A back-end database at the website mapping cookie IDs to user session history and preferences.

2.2.5 & 2.2.6 Web Caching and the Conditional GET

A Web cache (or proxy server) satisfies HTTP requests on behalf of origin Web servers. It has its own local storage, keeping copies of recently requested objects.

🎯 Classic Exam Calculation: Web Caching Delay Improvement (Slides Worked Example)
Suppose average object size is L = 100 Kbits, request rate is 15 req/s. Access link is R = 1.54 Mbps, and RTT from edge router to origin server is 2 seconds.
  • Average arrival rate of bits: 15 × 100 Kbits = 1.50 Mbps.
  • Access link utilization without cache:
    Utilization = 1.50 Mbps1.54 Mbps = 0.974  (97.4\%)
    Queuing delay is in minutes/seconds; total response time is enormous.
  • Now install an institutional Web cache with hit rate h = 0.40 (40%):
    • 40% of requests are satisfied locally over LAN in < 10 ms.
    • Traffic on the 1.54 Mbps access link drops by 40%: new arrival rate = 0.60 × 1.50 = 0.90 Mbps.
    • New access link utilization: 0.901.54 = 0.584  (58.4\%).
    • Average end-to-end response time drops from multiple seconds to:
    davg = 0.4 × (0.01 s) + 0.6 × (2.01 s) ≈ 1.2 seconds
    A dramatic improvement without buying expensive link bandwidth!

To prevent serving stale data, the cache issues a Conditional GET:

  1. The cache sends a GET request containing: If-Modified-Since: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT.
  2. If the object has not changed, the server replies: HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified with an empty entity body, saving link bandwidth!

2.2.7 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

  • HTTP/1.1 HOL Blocking: If a large or slow object is at the head of a pipelined connection, all following objects are delayed behind it.
  • HTTP/2: Eliminates application-layer Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking by dividing messages into independent binary frames and multiplexing multiple bidirectional request/response streams over a single TCP connection. Also adds server push and stream prioritization.
  • HTTP/3: While HTTP/2 solved application HOL blocking, TCP packet loss still stalled all multiplexed streams at the transport layer. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (built on top of UDP), providing independent per-stream loss recovery and zero-RTT connection establishment.

A. It specifies the client host's MAC address
B. It is mandatory for virtual hosting and caching, allowing one physical server with one IP address to host multiple domain names
C. It sets the TCP port number

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.3

§2.3 File Transfer: FTP

Out-of-band control on port 21 vs data transfer on port 20

The File Transfer Protocol (FTP, RFC 959) transfers files between a client host and a remote server. While both HTTP and FTP transfer files, FTP operates under a unique architectural design:

📘 Out-of-Band Control: Port 21 vs Port 20
FTP uses two parallel TCP connections:
  1. Control Connection (TCP Port 21): Used for sending user identification, password, directory commands, and file transfer commands. Remains open throughout the entire multi-file user session.
  2. Data Connection (TCP Port 20): Created anew for every single file transfer. When the transfer of a file (or directory listing) completes, the data connection is immediately closed.
Because FTP sends its control information over a completely separate connection from its data, FTP control is called out-of-band (in contrast to HTTP, which is in-band because request headers and file payloads share the exact same connection).

FTP Session State

Unlike stateless HTTP, an FTP server is stateful. The server maintains state about the client: current working directory, authenticated user identity, and active data port bindings.

🎯 Common FTP Commands and Status Replies
  • USER username: Sends username. Server replies 331 User name okay, need password.
  • PASS password: Sends password. Server replies 230 User logged in, proceed.
  • LIST: Requests directory listing (sent over a new data connection).
  • RETR filename: Retrieves (downloads) a file from server.
  • STOR filename: Stores (uploads) a file onto server.
Self-Check Question 1 §2.3 Concept Review
Why is FTP's control connection described as 'out-of-band'?
A. It uses UDP instead of TCP
B. It uses a separate TCP connection (port 21) from the data transfer connection (port 20)
C. It bypasses operating system sockets
D. It only works on wireless networks
Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.4

§2.4 Electronic Mail in the Internet

SMTP protocol exchange, mail message formats, and mail access (POP3 vs IMAP vs Webmail)

Internet email consists of three major architectural components: user agents, mail servers, and the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP, RFC 5321).

2.4.1 SMTP and the 6-Step Alice-to-Bob Mail Path

Suppose Alice wants to send an email to Bob:

  1. Alice composes a message in her user agent and clicks Send.
  2. Alice's user agent sends the message to her sender mail server over SMTP (or HTTP), where it is placed in the message queue.
  3. The client side of SMTP running on Alice's mail server opens a TCP connection to Bob's mail server on port 25.
  4. After an initial SMTP handshake, Alice's mail server transmits the message over the TCP connection.
  5. Bob's mail server deposits the arriving message into Bob's mailbox on disk.
  6. Bob retrieves the message from his mailbox using a mail access protocol (POP3, IMAP, or HTTP).
🎯 SMTP Command Exchange Protocol Trace (Study Guide P13)
SMTP command phases occur in a strict, prescribed sequence:
  1. Handshaking Phase:
    • Server: 220 mail.bob.com ESMTP ready
    • Client: HELO mail.alice.com
    • Server: 250 Hello mail.alice.com, pleased to meet you
  2. Transfer Phase:
    • Client: MAIL FROM: <alice@alice.com> → Server: 250 Sender OK
    • Client: RCPT TO: <bob@bob.com> → Server: 250 Recipient OK
    • Client: DATA → Server: 354 Start mail input; end with <CRLF>.<CRLF>
    • Client transmits header lines (To:, From:, Subject:) and message body lines.
    • Client transmits: . (a single line containing only a period) to mark end of message!
    • Server: 250 Message accepted for delivery
  3. Closure Phase:
    • Client: QUIT → Server: 221 mail.bob.com closing connection
⚖️ SMTP vs HTTP Comparison
  • Push vs Pull: HTTP is mainly a pull protocol (users pull web pages from server). SMTP is fundamentally a push protocol (sending mail server pushes mail to receiving mail server).
  • Character Encoding: SMTP requires all messages to be in 7-bit ASCII format (binary attachments must be encoded via Base64/MIME). HTTP allows arbitrary binary data.
  • Handling Multiple Objects: HTTP encapsulates each object in its own response message. SMTP places all text and attachments into a single multipart message.

2.4.4 Mail Access Protocols: POP3 vs IMAP vs Webmail

  • POP3 (Post Office Protocol 3, TCP Port 110): Simple. Client downloads messages from mailbox. Can operate in download-and-delete (messages deleted from server after download) or download-and-keep. Does not preserve folder states across multiple devices.
  • IMAP (Internet Mail Access Protocol, TCP Port 143): Advanced. Associates each message with a folder on the server. Maintains folder hierarchy and state across multiple devices (phone, laptop, desktop). Allows partial message download (e.g. headers only).
  • Webmail (HTTP/HTTPS, Port 443): Browser communicates with user's mail server via HTTP; the mail server communicates with remote mail servers via SMTP.

A. HELO → DATA → QUIT → MAIL FROM: → RCPT TO: → .
B. HELO (handshaking) → MAIL FROM: → RCPT TO: → DATA → message body → . (end message) → QUIT (closure)
C. MAIL FROM: → RCPT TO: → HELO → QUIT → DATA
D. DATA → HELO → MAIL FROM: → .

B. SMTP is strictly a push protocol, whereas retrieving messages requires a pull protocol like POP3, IMAP, or HTTP

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.5

§2.5 DNS—The Internet's Directory Service

Hierarchical architecture, iterative vs recursive queries, caching, and Resource Records

While humans prefer mnemonic names like www.kau.edu.sa, network routers identify destination interfaces using 32-bit IP addresses like 212.111.45.10. The Domain Name System (DNS, RFC 1034/1035) is the Internet's distributed, hierarchical directory service that translates hostnames to IP addresses. DNS runs over UDP port 53.

2.5.1 Services Provided by DNS

  1. Hostname-to-IP Translation: Translates human-friendly hostnames to IP addresses.
  2. Host Aliasing: A host with a complex canonical name (e.g. server-east-01.cdn.kau.edu.sa) can have one or more alias names (e.g. www.kau.edu.sa).
  3. Mail Server Aliasing: Enables clean email addresses (e.g. student@kau.edu.sa) by mapping the domain to the canonical mail server host (e.g. mail.kau.edu.sa).
  4. Load Distribution: Busy sites replicate across multiple server IP addresses. DNS rotates the order of returned IP addresses (round-robin DNS) to balance traffic.
💡 Why Is DNS Distributed Instead of Centralized?
A single centralized DNS server would suffer from fatal limitations:
  • Single Point of Failure: If the central server crashes, the entire global Internet stops working!
  • Traffic Volume: A single server would have to handle hundreds of billions of queries per second.
  • Distant Centralized Database: Queries from across the globe would experience enormous propagation delays.
  • Maintenance: Storing and updating all global records on one machine is administratively impossible.

2.5.2 The DNS Hierarchy

  • Root DNS Servers: 13 logical root server IP addresses worldwide (named A through M), managed by 12 distinct organizations. Each logical address is replicated across hundreds of physical servers using anycast routing.
  • Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers: Responsible for generic top-level domains (.com, .org, .edu, .gov) and country code domains (.sa, .uk, .jp).
  • Authoritative DNS Servers: Every organization with publicly accessible hosts must provide authoritative DNS records mapping its hostnames to IPs.
  • Local DNS Server (Default Resolver): Does not strictly belong to the hierarchy. Each ISP or university operates a local DNS server (e.g. via DHCP). When a host issues a DNS query, the query is sent directly to its local DNS server, which acts as a proxy to query the hierarchy.
🌳 Interactive Iterated DNS Resolution Trace (8 Messages)
Study Guide P14 Trace

Trace how a client at engineering.nyu.edu resolves gaia.cs.umass.edu using standard iterative queries:

Step 1: Host to Local DNS Server
Client host at engineering.nyu.edu queries its Local DNS Server (dns.nyu.edu) for gaia.cs.umass.edu. This query is recursive (local DNS takes responsibility to resolve it).

2.5.3 DNS Resource Records (RR)

DNS servers store Resource Records (RRs), which are 4-tuples: (Name, Value, Type, TTL).

RR Type Name Field Value Field Description & Example
Type A Hostname IPv4 Address Standard hostname-to-IP mapping: (dns1.abc.com, 10.1.2.3, A)
Type NS Domain Name Authoritative Hostname Identifies authoritative name server for domain: (abc.com, dns1.abc.com, NS)
Type CNAME Alias Hostname Canonical Hostname Canonical name for an alias: (shop.xyz.com, east7.backup.xyz.com, CNAME)
Type MX Domain Name Mail Server Hostname Specifies mail server for domain: (abc.com, mail.abc.com, MX)
📘 DNS Caching & TTL
When a local DNS server resolves a query, it caches the mapping locally. If another query for the same host arrives, it answers immediately from cache without querying root or TLD servers! Each record carries a TTL (Time-To-Live) determining when it must be purged. If a host changes its IP address before TTL expires, cached mappings are temporarily out of date (DNS provides best-effort consistency).

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.6

§2.6 Peer-to-Peer Applications & Video Streaming

P2P file distribution time equations, BitTorrent, DASH, and CDN architectures

Peer-to-Peer (P2P) systems leverage user end systems to distribute data directly without requiring dedicated server infrastructure.

2.6.1 File Distribution Time: Client-Server vs P2P

Consider distributing a file of size F bits to N peers. Let us be the server upload rate, dmin = mini di be the minimum peer download rate, and ui be peer i's upload rate:

🧮 Minimum Distribution Time Formulas (§2.6.1)
Client-Server Architecture:
DCS ≥ max( N ⋅ Fus,  Fdmin )
As N increases, server upload capacity is fixed at us; distribution time grows linearly with N!

Peer-to-Peer Architecture:
DP2P ≥ max( Fus,  Fdmin,  N ⋅ Fus + ∑i=1N ui )
P2P is self-scaling: each new peer brings its own upload capacity ui. As N → ∈fty, DP2P approaches a constant bound!
⚡ Interactive P2P vs Client-Server Distribution Calculator
Live Math Comparison

2.6.2 BitTorrent Architecture

  • Torrent: The collection of all peers participating in the distribution of a particular file.
  • Tracker: An infrastructure node that tracks active peers in the swarm and returns peer IP addresses to newcomers.
  • Chunks: The file is split into equal-size chunks (typically 256 KBytes).
  • Churn: Peers join and leave the torrent intermittently.
  • Rarest-First Strategy: A peer queries its neighbors to determine which chunk is least common among them, and requests that chunk first to equalize chunk distribution.
  • Tit-for-Tat Incentive (Unchoking): A peer measures download rates and sends chunks to the top 4 peers that provide data at the highest rate (evaluated every 10 seconds).
  • Optimistic Unchoking: Every 30 seconds, a peer randomly selects one additional peer to unchoke, giving newcomers a chance to earn a top-4 spot!

2.6.3 Video Streaming and DASH

Video accounts for over 70% of Internet traffic. Video is a sequence of images displayed at a constant rate (e.g. 24 or 30 frames/sec).

  • Continuous Playout Constraint: Once playout begins, frames must be displayed continuously according to original video timing. If network delay varies (jitter) and a frame arrives late, playout freezes (buffering stall!).
  • Client Playout Buffer & Delay: The client stores incoming video chunks in a local buffer for a few seconds before beginning playout. This buffer absorbs variations in packet delay.
  • DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP):
    • Video is encoded at multiple different bitrates (e.g. 240p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) and divided into multi-second chunks.
    • The server provides a Manifest File (MPD) listing the URLs and bitrates for all chunks.
    • The client measures available bandwidth and dynamically requests chunks at the highest possible quality without stalling.

2.6.4 Content Distribution Networks (CDNs)

Why can a single massive "mega-server" not stream video to millions of global users? (1) Single point of failure; (2) Network congestion around the server's access link; (3) Long propagation paths to distant users; (4) Redundant copies of the same video repeatedly cross the same transit links.

A Content Distribution Network (CDN) distributes server copies across geographically distributed nodes:

  1. Enter Deep (Akamai Philosophy): Deploy thousands of server clusters inside thousands of access ISPs around the world, getting as close to users as possible.
  2. Bring Home (Limelight Philosophy): Build fewer, larger clusters located at Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) and private peering points.
  3. DNS CNAME Redirection: When a user requests video.netcinema.com, NetCinema's authoritative DNS server returns a CNAME pointing to kingcdn.com, and KingCDN's name server directs the user to the nearest server cluster!
Self-Check Question 1 §2.6 Concept Review

A. It contains the cryptographic SSL private keys
B. It lists the URLs of video chunks available encoded at various bitrates, allowing the client to adapt quality dynamically
C. It acts as a BitTorrent tracker
D. It stores user cookie passwords

Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.7

§2.7 Socket Programming: Building Network Applications

Building Python network clients and servers with UDP and TCP

We examine the standard Python socket API for creating networked applications. A network application consists of a pair of programs (a client program and a server program) residing on two different end systems.

2.7.1 Socket Programming with UDP (Connectionless)

In UDP, there is no initial handshake. The sender attaches the destination IP address and port number to every datagram:

UDPClient.py
from socket import *
serverName = '192.168.1.50'
serverPort = 12000
# Create UDP socket (AF_INET = IPv4, SOCK_DGRAM = UDP)
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
message = input('Input lowercase sentence: ')
# Send datagram with attached destination address
clientSocket.sendto(message.encode(), (serverName, serverPort))
# Read response datagram and server address
modifiedMessage, serverAddress = clientSocket.recvfrom(2048)
print(modifiedMessage.decode())
clientSocket.close()
UDPServer.py
from socket import *
serverPort = 12000
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
# Bind socket to local port 12000
serverSocket.bind(('', serverPort))
print('UDP Server is ready to receive')
while True:
    message, clientAddress = serverSocket.recvfrom(2048)
    modifiedMessage = message.decode().upper()
    serverSocket.sendto(modifiedMessage.encode(), clientAddress)

2.7.2 Socket Programming with TCP (Connection-Oriented)

In TCP, client and server perform a 3-way handshake before transmitting data. The TCP server employs two distinct sockets:

  1. Welcoming Socket: Listens for incoming connection requests on a well-known port (e.g. 12000).
  2. Connection Socket: Created anew by serverSocket.accept() specifically for that individual client connection!
TCPClient.py
from socket import *
serverName = '192.168.1.50'
serverPort = 12000
# Create TCP socket (SOCK_STREAM = TCP)
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
# Initiate 3-way handshake
clientSocket.connect((serverName, serverPort))
sentence = input('Input lowercase sentence: ')
# Send byte stream (no destination address needed!)
clientSocket.send(sentence.encode())
modifiedSentence = clientSocket.recv(1024)
print('From Server:', modifiedSentence.decode())
clientSocket.close()
TCPServer.py
from socket import *
serverPort = 12000
# Create welcoming socket
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
serverSocket.bind(('', serverPort))
serverSocket.listen(1) # Listen for connections
print('TCP Server is ready to receive')
while True:
    # Accept creates dedicated connection socket!
    connectionSocket, addr = serverSocket.accept()
    sentence = connectionSocket.recv(1024).decode()
    capitalizedSentence = sentence.upper()
    connectionSocket.send(capitalizedSentence.encode())
    connectionSocket.close()
Self-Check Question 1 §2.7 Concept Review
In TCP socket programming, what is the role of the welcoming socket vs the connection socket?
A. The welcoming socket performs encryption while the connection socket sends plaintext
B. The welcoming socket remains listening on the known port for connection requests, while accept() spawns a dedicated connection socket for that specific client
C. The welcoming socket runs on the client and the connection socket runs on the server
D. The welcoming socket uses UDP and the connection socket uses TCP
Chapter 2: Application Layer • Section 2.8

§2.8 Chapter 2 Summary & Exam Practice Problems (P9–P16)

Complete worked solutions to all 8 Midterm Study Guide Practice Problems plus Textbook Problems

Master these 8 practice problems from the official CPCS-371 Midterm Study Guide covering Chapter 2:

📝 Practice Problem P9: Architectures and Processes
Study Guide P9

Problem:

(a) Give two properties of the server in the client-server paradigm and two properties of peers in a P2P architecture.
(b) In a P2P file-sharing session, which process is the client and which is the server?
(c) Why is a host's IP address not enough to identify the receiving process?

(a) Server properties: Always on; fixed permanent IP address; typically housed in dedicated data centers.
Peer properties: Arbitrary end systems communicate directly; no dedicated central server; self-scalable (peers provide service capacity as well as demand); intermittently connected with changing IP addresses.
(b) The peer that initiates contact and downloads chunks is the client process; the peer that receives the request and uploads chunks is the server process.
(c) A single host may run multiple network applications simultaneously (e.g. web server, email client, SSH session). The 32-bit IP address identifies only the physical host; the 16-bit port number is required to identify the specific process/socket.
📝 Practice Problem P10: Transport Service Needs Matching
Study Guide P10

Problem: For (i) file download, (ii) Internet telephony, (iii) e-mail, and (iv) an interactive online game, state whether the application tolerates data loss, whether it is time-sensitive, and which transport protocol it typically uses.

• (i) File Download: No loss tolerated; not time-sensitive; uses TCP.
• (ii) Internet Telephony (VoIP): Loss-tolerant; time-sensitive (10's–150 ms); uses UDP (or TCP).
• (iii) E-mail: No loss tolerated; not time-sensitive; uses TCP.
• (iv) Interactive Game: Loss-tolerant; time-sensitive (10's–100 ms); uses UDP (or TCP).
📝 Practice Problem P11: Dissecting HTTP Request Headers
Study Guide P11

Problem: A web browser transmits the following request:

GET /cpcs371/notes/ch2.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.edu
Connection: keep-alive

(a) What is the full URL of the requested object?
(b) What does Connection: keep-alive indicate?
(c) The server replies HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found. What does this mean?
(d) Which HTTP method sends form input in the entity body, and which method requests only headers?

(a) Full URL: http://www.example.edu/cpcs371/notes/ch2.html (Host name + Path name).
(b) Connection: keep-alive: The client requests a persistent HTTP connection; the server should keep the underlying TCP connection open for subsequent requests.
(c) 404 Not Found: The server successfully received the request, but the requested document does not exist at the specified path on the server.
(d) POST sends form input in the entity body; HEAD requests only the response header lines without the entity body.
📝 Practice Problem P12: Non-Persistent Response Time & Cookies
Study Guide P12

Problem:

(a) The RTT between client and server is 60 ms and transmitting an object takes 15 ms. With non-persistent HTTP, how long does it take to receive one object from the moment the client starts opening the connection?
(b) HTTP is stateless. Describe how the four cookie components let an online bookstore recognize a returning customer one week later.

Part (a): With non-persistent HTTP:
dresponse = 2 × RTT + dtrans = (2 × 60 ms) + 15 ms = 120 + 15 = 135 ms
(1 RTT to open TCP connection + 1 RTT for HTTP request/response header + 15 ms transmission).
Part (b):
  1. On the first visit, the server creates a unique user identification number and creates a matching entry in its back-end database.
  2. The server includes the header Set-Cookie: ID in its HTTP response message.
  3. The client browser saves the cookie ID line in its local cookie file.
  4. One week later, every request from that browser to the site automatically includes the header Cookie: ID. The server looks up the ID in its database, retrieving the user's shopping cart and preferences!
📝 Practice Problem P13: Ordering SMTP Commands
Study Guide P13

Problem: Put the following SMTP items in correct sequential order and state which phase of the transfer each belongs to: DATA, HELO, QUIT, RCPT TO:, MAIL FROM:, a line containing only ..

1. HELO → Handshaking Phase (client introduces its domain to server).
2. MAIL FROM: → Transfer Phase (identifies sender mailbox).
3. RCPT TO: → Transfer Phase (identifies recipient mailbox).
4. DATA → Transfer Phase (initiates message body text).
5. . (single period line) → Transfer Phase (terminates message input).
6. QUIT → Closure Phase (terminates TCP connection).
📝 Practice Problem P14: DNS Resolution & Resource Records
Study Guide P14

Problem:

(a) A host at engineering.nyu.edu needs the IP of gaia.cs.umass.edu. With an iterated query and empty cache, list the 8 DNS messages exchanged.
(b) State the Resource Record Type for each:
 • (dns1.abc.com, 10.1.2.3, ?)
 • (abc.com, dns1.abc.com, ?)
 • (shop.xyz.com, east7.backup.xyz.com, ?)
 • (abc.com, mail.abc.com, ?)
(c) Why can a cached mapping be out of date, and what limits how long it stays cached?

Part (a): 8 messages:
  1. Host → Local DNS server (query gaia.cs.umass.edu)
  2. Local DNS → Root DNS server
  3. Root DNS → Local DNS (referral to .edu TLD server)
  4. Local DNS → .edu TLD server
  5. TLD server → Local DNS (referral to umass.edu authoritative server)
  6. Local DNS → umass.edu authoritative server
  7. Authoritative server → Local DNS (returns IP address of gaia.cs.umass.edu)
  8. Local DNS → Host (delivers IP address)
Part (b):
• (dns1.abc.com, 10.1.2.3, A) → Type A (Hostname to IPv4).
• (abc.com, dns1.abc.com, NS) → Type NS (Authoritative name server for domain).
• (shop.xyz.com, east7.backup.xyz.com, CNAME) → Type CNAME (Canonical name for alias).
• (abc.com, mail.abc.com, MX) → Type MX (Mail server for domain).
Part (c): Name servers cache records to reduce latency. If a host changes its IP address, the cache does not know until the TTL (Time-To-Live) timer expires. DNS provides best-effort consistency.
📝 Practice Problem P15: P2P and BitTorrent Mechanisms
Study Guide P15

Problem:

(a) What does "self-scalability" mean in P2P?
(b) What is a torrent, and what is churn?
(c) How does tit-for-tat reward peers that upload?

(a) Self-scalability: Each new peer that joins the system brings new service demand (downloading), but also contributes new service capacity (uploading). Therefore, total system capacity grows proportionally with the number of users.
(b) A torrent is the group of all peers participating in the distribution of a particular file. Churn refers to the frequent, unpredictable joining and leaving of peers.
(c) Under tit-for-tat, a peer unchokes (sends data to) the top 4 peers that provide data to it at the highest upload rate. Thus, peers that upload generously to others are rewarded by becoming top partners of others and receiving chunks at high rates in return.
📝 Practice Problem P16: Video Streaming, DASH, and CDNs
Study Guide P16

Problem:

(a) Why does a video client buffer data before starting playout?
(b) What does a DASH manifest file contain?
(c) Give three reasons why one huge "mega-server" cannot stream to millions of users.

(a) Network packet delay varies dynamically (jitter), but video playback must adhere to the continuous playout constraint. A client-side buffer absorbs delay variations so the video does not freeze.
(b) A DASH manifest file (MPD) contains the URLs of video chunks, each encoded at various bitrates and resolutions.
(c) Any three of:
  1. Single point of failure: If the mega-server or its data center fails, the entire service goes down.
  2. Network congestion bottleneck: The access links leading to the mega-server become severely congested.
  3. Long propagation paths: Distant international users experience high latency and packet loss.
  4. Wasted transit bandwidth: Redundant copies of the exact same video stream repeatedly cross the same transit links.

Chapter 3: Transport Layer • Section 3.1

§3.1 Transport-Layer Services

Relationship between Transport and Network Layers, and the Household Postal Analogy

A transport-layer protocol provides for logical communication between application processes running on different hosts. From an application process's perspective, it appears as if the hosts were directly connected, whereas in reality they may be on opposite sides of the planet connected by dozens of routers and diverse physical links.

Transport-layer protocols are implemented strictly in the end systems (hosts), not in network routers. Core routers inspect only network-layer fields (IP addresses); they do not inspect or modify transport-layer segments.

💡 The 12-Kids Household Postal Analogy (Kurose & Ross §3.1)
Consider two large family households: one on the East Coast with 12 kids (including cousin Ann), and one on the West Coast with 12 kids (including cousin Bill).
  • The kids write letters to each other every week (Application messages).
  • In each house, one kid (Ann on East Coast, Bill on West Coast) collects letters from all siblings and distributes arriving letters to individual brothers and sisters (Transport-layer protocol: multiplexing & demultiplexing).
  • The postal trucks and mail carriers transport mail bags between the two houses (Network-layer protocol: host-to-host delivery).
Key take-away: Ann and Bill do not drive mail trucks between cities (they operate only inside the house), nor does the postal carrier deliver mail directly into the hands of a specific child in their bedroom! Transport protocols provide process-to-process communication on top of host-to-host network delivery.
Figure 3.1 — Transport-layer process-to-process communication vs Network-layer host-to-host delivery (§3.1).
Self-Check Question 1 §3.1 Concept Review
In the 12-kids household postal analogy, what corresponds to the transport-layer protocol?
A. The letters written by the children
B. The postal carrier driving the truck between cities
C. Ann and Bill collecting and distributing letters within their respective houses
D. The envelope paper and ink
Chapter 3: Transport Layer • Section 3.2

§3.2 Multiplexing and Demultiplexing

Port numbers, 2-tuple connectionless demux vs 4-tuple connection-oriented demux

A destination host receives IP datagrams from the network layer. Each datagram carries a transport segment. Delivering the segment data to the correct application socket is called demultiplexing. Gathering data chunks from multiple application sockets at the source host, prefixing them with transport headers, and passing them to the network layer is called multiplexing.

Port Numbers (RFC 1700)

Port numbers are 16-bit integers ranging from 0 to 65535:

  • Well-Known Ports (0 to 1023): Standard services (HTTP: 80, HTTPS: 443, DNS: 53, SMTP: 25, FTP: 20/21, SSH: 22). Restricted to privileged/root processes.
  • Registered Ports (1024 to 49151): Registered for vendor applications.
  • Dynamic / Private / Ephemeral Ports (49152 to 65535): Assigned automatically by the OS to client processes upon socket creation.
📘 Connectionless (UDP) Demultiplexing: 2-Tuple
A UDP socket is identified solely by a 2-tuple:
(Destination IP Address,  Destination Port Number)
If two UDP datagrams originate from completely different source IP addresses or different source port numbers, but have the same destination IP and destination port number, both datagrams will be directed to the exact same destination socket!
📘 Connection-Oriented (TCP) Demultiplexing: 4-Tuple
A TCP socket is identified by a 4-tuple:
(Source IP,  Source Port,  Destination IP,  Destination Port)
When a TCP segment arrives at a host, the OS uses all four fields to demultiplex the segment to the specific connection socket.
Exam Example (Study Guide P17b): A web server listens on port 80 (welcoming socket). Client A (IP: 192.168.1.10, Port: 4001) and Client B (IP: 192.168.1.20, Port: 4001) both connect to port 80. Although both clients chose source port 4001 and destination port 80, the server creates two separate connection sockets because their Source IP addresses differ!
Self-Check Question 1 §3.2 Concept Review
Two UDP datagrams arrive at Host C on destination port 5353: one from (Host A, Port 4001) and one from (Host B, Port 4002). How many sockets at C receive them?
A. Two distinct sockets
B. One socket: UDP demultiplexes by destination port only, so both datagrams go to the same socket bound to 5353
C. Zero: the second packet is rejected as a duplicate
D. Four sockets
Self-Check Question 2 §3.2 Concept Review
Two TCP clients connect to a Web server on port 80: one from (Host A, Port 4001) and one from (Host B, Port 4001). How many connection sockets are created at the server?
A. One shared connection socket
B. Two connection sockets (plus the welcoming socket), because TCP uses the 4-tuple and their source IPs differ
C. Zero, because source ports clash
D. Three connection sockets
Chapter 3: Transport Layer • Section 3.3

§3.3 Connectionless Transport: UDP

UDP segment structure, advantages, and the 16-bit Internet Checksum algorithm

UDP (User Datagram Protocol, RFC 768) is the minimal transport protocol. It takes application messages, attaches an 8-byte header, and hands the segment to the network layer.

Why Would an Application Choose UDP over TCP?

  1. Finer Application Control Over What Data Is Sent, and When: UDP does not throttle sending rates via congestion control. Real-time applications can pump data at a constant rate and tolerate minor packet loss.
  2. No Connection Establishment Delay: UDP does not introduce any connection 3-way handshake delay. This is why DNS uses UDP (name lookup completes in 1 RTT).
  3. No Connection State: TCP maintains receive/send buffers, congestion parameters, and sequence numbers. A server running UDP can support vastly more active clients simultaneously because it maintains zero state.
  4. Small Header Overhead: UDP header is only 8 bytes, whereas TCP's base header is 20 bytes.
Figure 3.2 — Bit-accurate UDP Segment Header (8 bytes total overhead) (§3.3.1).

The 16-Bit Internet Checksum Algorithm

🧮 1's Complement Checksum Calculation Steps (Study Guide P18)
  1. Treat all 16-bit words in the segment (including header and pseudo-header) as unsigned 16-bit integers.
  2. Add them together using binary addition.
  3. End-Around Carry (Wraparound): If a carry bit spills out of the 16th most significant bit, add it back to the least significant bit.
  4. Take the 1's complement of the wrapped sum (invert every bit: flip 0s to 1s and 1s to 0s). This is the checksum stored in the header.
  5. Receiver Verification: The receiver adds all 16-bit words plus the checksum. If no bits were corrupted, the result must be all 1s (1111 1111 1111 1111 = 0xFFFF)! If any single bit is 0, an error occurred.
🧮 Live 16-Bit Internet Checksum Calculator
Study Guide P18 Worked Math

Enter two 16-bit hex words (e.g. from P18: 5CA3 and C675) to see the live binary addition, wraparound carry, and bit inversion:
